en: Their knees bending to the ground,
Pleading for the wrestler's life,
All the beks ran.
Before they could intervene,
Before they could plead for his life,
Semetey, full of anger,
Seized him by the waist and swung him,
With a sharp crack, the wrestler
He dashed to the ground.
The boy unleashed terror.
One of Toobalban's arms,
He tore clean out,
With this, Toobalban
Now lay dead.
The eight khans who came to the feast,
There were dignitaries, there were khans,
All the honored people were there,
There were keen-eared men who knew the news,
Of the adventures of fierce Manas,
There were elders who had seen his ways.
To Kakan Khan's Beijing,
Driving them there, mighty Manas,
Had he not had them slaughtered?
All those old grudge-bearers were there.
They began whispering together,
Speaking words of great mischief,
Trampling the places they walked,
All the khans who came
Of Manas gone to the other world,
Gossiped and spoke ill.
They could not bear to see the boy,
Their thoughts grew ever more wicked.
The ground they trod became a hollow,
They turned staunch enemies of the boy,
Trampling the places they walked,
They prattled and spoke ill.
Without looking all around,
Without sparing the boy's life at all:
“His father Manas was a hero,
Just such a rash lion was he.
While his khan-father lived,
He used to oppress Kokand,
Beating us, making us cry out,
Six thousand beaver pelts, a thousand ingots,
He used to take as tribute every month.
Unable to bear his tribute,
The Six Cities, Kokand, Margalang,
Used to weep bitterly.
While his father Manas lived,
Throughout the face of the earth,
He used to bring calamity.
Unable to bear his wrath,
Before his khan-father Manas,
Everyone used to weep.
He set fire to the sedge-covered land,
Offspring of the man cursed to burn,
He set the grassland smoldering,
Offspring of the terror,
He poured blood into clear water,
This is the heedless one himself!
In the end the boy will bring no good,
If he lives, he will leave no peace.
Now he has reached the age of twelve;
When he reaches seventeen,
He will never leave us unharmed.
He will not let us turn the plow,
He will not let us dwell upon this earth.
When springtime comes,
He will not let us ride a maned filly.
When autumn comes,
He will not let us eat a fat-tailed lamb.
He will not let us fit the yoke peg,
He will not let us plow in spring.
He will not let us break the earth,
He will not let us scatter a double handful of seed.
He will not let us turn the plow,
He will not let us dwell in this land.
He will plunder our precious goods.
If this orphan lives,
He will wreak great mischief.
Whoever opposes him,
Seizing them, the wretched orphan
Will offer them as a sacrifice.
He will scatter the four kinds of livestock.
This orphan, the lord's son,
Will raid and take the mares.
If we happen to come near,
He will strike our brains in all directions!
Better that upon Bukhara
We bring a cunning scheme.
Deceiving them into agreement,
Better that we ask for the orphan,
And take him as a hostage.
Margalang, midway in the land,
Let us somehow ask to take him there.
With thimble mouths and camel-calf eyes,
Gathering swaying girls,
Gathering lovely craftswomen,
Their waists a handspan, their faces moonlike,
Let us gather the distinguished ones.
If the boy wishes to take them,
Let us marry five to him.
After doing this for the boy,
The millet beer poured into the wooden vat,
Let it ferment, you fools.
Make it stronger, eight khans.
The millet beer poured into the leather bucket,
Mix into it without stint,
That burning poison.
When the boy is drunk,
Let us cut off his head,
Let us offer him as a sacrifice.
Cutting off his head and tying it up,
To Abyke and Kobosh,
Let us go with glad tidings.
‘The head of the enemy who defied you,’ we shall say,
The many cattle amassed as treasure,
The countless livestock left by Manas,
Let us take as our reward for the news.
If God grants it, in this way,
Let us grow rich and live at ease.”
The eight khans who came to the feast
Spoke such words,
Made their pledge firm.
Chewing grains of white wheat,
Holding the Holy Word,
They slaughtered a white-gray mare.
The Holy Word, the great Quran,
They held firmly to their breasts.
Six from each khan,
Their spokesmen came forward.
Eloquent, gifted with speech,
Saying more than enough,
Unsparing in their cunning,
Before his grandfather Temir Khan,
They now laid weighty words.
The envoys of the eight khans,
For the formidable orphan boy,
The heir left by King Manas,
Now asked to take him as a hostage.
Before Temir Khan,
Smooth of speech, honey-tongued,
One of the eloquent men now came:
“Greetings upon greetings, peace be upon you,
My illustrious khan and elder brother!
Father of all the people,
Consider these words, my elder!
A wrestler and a lion,
You have an exceptional son.
That son of yours, my lord,
May his coal turn to gold,
May his life stretch far.
The Russians on his right,
Your son is one who would mow them down.
The Chinese on the uplands,
He is a hero who would slaughter them.
If unbelievers press us and cause strife,
If they put our precious lives to the test,
If an enemy fixes a firm gaze upon us,
If hardship comes upon our precious lives,
He is a son whose words would help.
If unbelievers press us still harder,
He is a son whose strength would help.
Consent to these words this year,
The boy whom you cherish,
Give him to us as a hostage this year.
To Margalang, midway in the land,
Let us take your boy.
As the people's darling,
Let us establish him as a hostage.
Let us gather the finest beauties.
From children of khans, of pure lineage,
Let us marry seven to him.”
Rash Temir Khan,
To the spokesmen's words,
Was ready to consent, did you see?
His boy as a hostage,
He was ready to give, did you see?
The hostage boy Semetey,
Let us leave him there for now.
The afflicted old woman Chyiyrdy,
The mother who bore Manas,
Let us begin to tell of her.
Mighty Manas, khan of the world,
Had he not died?
Most terrible of all, a grievous ordeal,
For twelve years unable to rise,
With no strength to get up,
Had she not sunk low?
When her noble son died,
Had she not suffered humiliation?
From all the villains,
Suffering much humiliation like a dog,
Had she not endured oppression?
Wishing to die from shame,
The old woman stayed alive,
Because Semetey was there.
“Plump, gray-pied goshawk,” she said,
Chyiyrdy wept and wailed.
“Morning star left by Manas,” she said,
Too full of sorrow to stay still.
Her heart filled with anxiety,
The old woman placed her hope
In the boy left by her son.
She had reached ninety-five.
Her appointed death had not yet come.
Until twelve years had passed,
Until the boy reached twelve,
She had not seen Semetey.
She heard news from those who came.
“Taking after his father, in Bukhara,
He has excelled,” she heard.
Hearing of his excellence, in distress,
For six days without eating,
The venerable old woman Chyiyrdy
Lay down in hurt resentment.
The old woman could find no way,
And pleaded with Kanykey:
“Oh, Kanykey, my foal,
The dear bird called a wild duck
Flies to the steppe without turning back.
I have not died of grief,
Thinking of the child born from my womb.
The wretched bird called a harrier
Swoops down for food.
That I have not yet died—
My poor child, it is for you.
The dear bird called a wild duck,
I let a goshawk devour it.
The orphan I had honored,
Fleeing here to Bukhara,
I had him called Temir Khan's son.
My wretched fortune, I fed it to a bird.
The only one born from my womb,
Coming destitute to Bukhara,
I had him called Ismayyl's son.
A dug pit, a deep trench—
Oh, Kanykey, my foal,
Our misery boils and seethes.
This year I shall die before my destined time,
Kanykey, my child,
I shall see the face of the next world.
The orphan left by the Magnanimous One,
On what day shall I see him?
The hoof left by the winged steed,
The tireless swift horse, my light,
Show him plainly before my eyes,
The orphan left by the goshawk.
God has divided my thoughts.
When shall I see, Kanykey,
The child born from my womb?
Oh, Kanykey, my foal,
I wish to see Semetey.
If I do not see Semetey,
This year, my child, I wish to die.”
